why: Counting subsets with sum exactly k is the same take-or-skip table as 0/1 knapsack, but the initial values change the meaning: ways[0] = 1 (the empty subset) and every other sum starts at 0, so only exact totals are ever counted. Contrast 'at most W', where every cell starts at 0 value.
hints: For each element you either include it or not, so ways after an element = ways without it + ways that reach s - v.
ways[s] = number of subsets of the elements seen so far with sum exactly s. Initialise ways[0] = 1 and the rest 0; that initial row is what says 'exactly'.
For each v, loop s from k down to v and add ways[s - v] into ways[s]. Answer ways[k]. O(n * k).
pitfalls: Zeros double the count: [2,0,2] with k=2 has 4 subsets. With v = 0 the loop adds ways[s] to itself, doubling every count, which is exactly right.
k = 0 always counts the empty subset.
Initialising every ways[s] to 1 would count 'sum at most s' style nonsense; only ways[0] is 1.
